en: Now, besides adding context and
participants to chat,
GitHub Copilot Chat also offers you these
slash commands, which you also see here on
my screen, and some other slash commands
to
quickly
invoke various functionalities that are
supported by GitHub Copilot.
So if I type a slash here, I'll actually see
some of these suggestions down here and also
up here.
For example,
I can use
@terminal/explain to explain some command I
currently have in my terminal or some
command I currently have
selected.
I can also, and that's sometimes even more
useful, use the inline chat and for example,
select some code
and then use a slash command here to quickly
invoke
a command, a feature if you wanna call it
like this, provided by GitHub Copilot
that will
take this selected code
into account or that will take this selected
code as a base.
For example, if I use /explain with this
code selected, I don't need to type anything
else.
I could to add more instructions or more
context,
but I can also run it like this to have this
code
be explained to me.
I could add more information if I wanted to
specify which kind of explanation I'm
looking for. But if I run it like this,
you see it will open up this little window
here and it will explain that code for me
here.
Of course, it can be a bit annoying to
browse that here, so I can always click View
in Chat, and I have the entire explanation
here in my chat now.
Now besides /explain, I could also run
/fix
if there is some problem with that code and
I want Copilot to fix it.
I also might want to add some text here then
where I describe the problem,
like I don't want to use the
logging package.
And it will now fix that code taking my
instruction into account and go back to the
print statement, for example.
And I could now accept this or discard it if
I don't want it. And here I'll discard it
because I'm happy with the logging package.
But that would've been one way of using this
fix command.
Now of course, I could have also described
my intent without fix, like, I don't want to
use the
logging package. And chances are high that
it would've worked as well,
as you can tell.
But by using
/fix, you're adding some extra context
again. And
using these AI chat tools is all about
context. It's always about adding the right
context in the right place because with this
/fix command, we make it very clear that we
wanna fix this code.
And therefore, for certain commands where
sometimes GitHub Copilot might
not always give us the right response, the
right result, adding little extra pieces of
context like this can make the difference,
which is why it's important to know about
it.
Now, another very useful slash command is
/tests, and we'll explore this in the next
lecture.
